instructions: Rinse the 2 1/2 cups rice in a strainer under cold water until the water runs mostly clear. Put it in a saucepan with 2 3/4 cups water and bring it to a boil over high heat. Turn the heat to low, cover the pan and cook for 15 minutes. Take it off the heat and keep the lid on until you're ready to serve.

Meanwhile, make the broth. Put 2 cups water and the 2 tsp dashi granules in a small saucepan and bring it to a simmer over medium heat. Stir in the 4 tsp sugar, 1/4 cup mirin and 1/4 cup soy sauce, then take it off the heat.
Cut the onion in half and slice it thin. Slice 2 of the green onions thin and keep them separate.
Trim any thick fat off the 4 boneless pork loin chops. Make small cuts every inch through the band of connective tissue between the fat and the meat, on both sides, so the pork stays flat in the oil.
Pound the chops with a meat mallet or rolling pin to an even 1/2 inch, then push them back into shape. Sprinkle both sides with the 1 tsp salt and 1/4 tsp pepper.
Set out three plates: the 1/4 cup flour on one, 2 of the eggs beaten with 1 tbsp of the oil on the next, and the 1 1/2 cups panko on the last.
Coat each chop in flour and shake off the extra. Dip it in the egg, then lay it in the panko and press so the crumbs stick on both sides. Set them on a tray while the oil heats.

Pour the rest of the oil into a heavy pot. It should be about 2 inches deep. Heat it over medium to 340°F. No thermometer? Drop in a crumb of panko: it should sink a little and float straight back up, sizzling.

Lower 2 of the cutlets in, laying them away from you. Stand back a little. They'll spatter. Fry them for 2 1/2 minutes without touching them, then flip them and cook the other side for 2 1/2 minutes, until deep golden brown.
Lift them out, hold them over the pot for a few seconds to drip, and set them on a wire rack. Skim out any loose crumbs, then fry the other 2 cutlets the same way.

You're cooking the pork to 145°F in the middle, so if you have a thermometer, check the thickest part. No thermometer? Cut into the center of one: the juices should run clear, with the middle just barely pink.
Slice each cutlet across into strips about 1 inch wide, keeping each one together in its shape.
Crack 3 of the remaining eggs into one bowl and the last 3 into another. Break the yolks and stir each bowl only a few strokes with chopsticks or a fork, so there are still streaks of white.
Spread half the sliced onion in a large frying pan that has a lid and pour in half the broth, about 1 cup. Cover and cook over medium heat until the onion is soft and see-through, about 4 minutes.
Lay 2 of the sliced cutlets on the onion. Cover and cook for 2 minutes, until the broth is bubbling around them.

Pour one bowl of egg over the cutlets and onion in a slow spiral, keeping away from the edges of the pan. Cover and cook for about 1 minute, until the egg is just set with the top still a little runny. Take the pan off the heat.
Divide half the rice between 2 large bowls. Slide one cutlet, with its egg and onion, onto each bowl and spoon the broth from the pan over the top.
Wipe out the pan and make the other 2 bowls the same way with the rest of the onion, the rest of the broth, the last 2 cutlets, the second bowl of egg and the rest of the rice.
Taste a spoonful of the broth from a bowl. If it's flat, sprinkle a pinch more salt over the egg.
Scatter the sliced green onions over the bowls and serve right away.
method_notes: All three simmer sliced onion in a sweet soy and dashi broth, warm the sliced cutlet in it, pour over loosely beaten egg, cover until it's barely set and slide the lot onto rice. Just One Cookbook starts from ready made tonkatsu, cooks two cutlets to a large pan and uses dashi, mirin, soy sauce and sugar; No Recipes sautés the onion in oil first and adds sake and a little starch to the sauce, and RecipeTin Japan fries the cutlets in the same recipe and cooks one bowl at a time in a small pan. This one follows Just One Cookbook's broth and two-at-a-time pan, and fries the cutlets first the way RecipeTin Japan does, since there's no leftover tonkatsu to start from.
